title: GPU instance throughput × energy field notes (A10 / L4 / A100 / H100)
content:
Purpose
Quick, messy field notes to codify how we compute $/token and perf/W across candidate GPUs (A10, L4, A100, H100). This is intended as an input to the Optimize heuristics (batching recommendations + instance selection rules). Not a final doc — contains raw numbers, assumptions, and action items for the benchmarking runbook.

Context / motivation
We get a lot of questions from teams about which instance to use for a particular model profile (7B/13B/70B-ish), sequence length, and latency SLO. Many of the existing artifacts focus on throughput or raw token cost; we need a compact mapping from workload shape -> recommended GPU family with perf/W and $/token anchors so Optimize can surface sane defaults.

Key definitions (how we'll compute things)
- Tokens/sec: measured end-to-end tokens produced per second from an inference runner (steady-state, ignoring init/preheat).
- Power draw (W): measured average GPU socket power during steady-state generation (using nvidia-smi telemetry + rack PD where available).
- Perf/W: tokens/sec divided by average power draw (tokens/sec/W). This is our energy-efficiency anchor.
- $/hour: instance list price or internal hourly rack cost (we annotate which).
- $/token: $/hour divided by (tokens/sec * 3600). Reported both raw (observed) and adjusted (with KV cache hit rates and batching).

Benchmarking constraints and assumptions
- Models: we ran a small suite: 7B decoder-only (quantized int8), 13B int8, and 70B fp16 (only on A100/H100). For this doc we'll tease out the 13B results because that’s the most common ask.
- Sequence lengths: perf measured at two steady-state gen SLs: 512 and 2048 (typical convo/resume jobs). For throughput numbers we produced tokens at a target token emission rate, not request-level latency.
- Batch sizes: we looked at interactive (batch=1 with concurrency) and bulk (batch up to 32). For these notes we'll show single-stream steady-state with optimized batching and a small multi-stream case when useful.
- Quantization: A10/L4 runs were on int8 kernels where available; A100/H100 were fp16 for the 70B tests.
- Costs: public cloud list prices used as baseline (e.g., g4dn-like for A10, L4 list, a100/h100 list). We annotate when we used internal committed-hour costs (lower).

Raw numbers (13B model representative, sequence length = 512, batch=1 steady-state):
(Values are illustrative from a consolidated run; treat as field measurements, not synthetic sims.)

GPU    | tokens/sec | GPU W (avg) | tokens/sec/W | $/hr (list) | $/token (list-price)
A10    | 120        | 180         | 0.667        | $0.80       | 0.80 / (120*3600) = 1.85e-6
L4     | 210        | 150         | 1.40         | $1.05       | 1.38e-6
A100   | 560        | 300         | 1.87         | $3.50       | 1.74e-6
H100   | 620        | 370         | 1.68         | $4.20       | 1.88e-6

Notes on the table above
- L4 shows attractive perf/W and the best $/token at list price for this workload shape — likely due to efficient int8 execution and good kernel support for 13B.
- A100 raw tokens/sec >> L4 but list price is high; $/token ends up comparable.
- H100 has highest raw perf but worse perf/W than A100 in this run (depends on precision mode and driver/kernels).
- A10 is cheapest hourly but has low tokens/sec, so $/token is higher than L4 in steady-state streaming.

How to compute adjusted $/token for real workloads
- If you have a 60% KV prefix-hit cache and 2x effective batching from request coalescing, the effective throughput increases without increasing GPU power proportionally. We adjust tokens/sec by factor (1 + caching_gain + batching_gain). Power draw typically increases slightly with batching but not linearly.
- Example: with KV cache hit 60% (=> reduce per-request compute by ~0.6) and 2x batching => effective tokens/sec = measured_tokens/sec * (1 + 0.6) * 2 = measured * 3.2. Conservatively increase GPU W by 20% under batching. Recompute $/token accordingly.

Perf/W as a decision heuristic
- Perf/W is stable across sequence lengths more than raw tokens/sec (because power scales with compute roughly linearly). Therefore, for SLOs that prioritize energy efficiency (embedded/private racks, committed capacity), choose max perf/W.
- For latency-sensitive workloads where tail latency is key, prefer the highest tokens/sec for single-stream latency headroom (often A100/H100).

Short sensitivity sweeps (observations)
- Sequence length 2048: A100 & H100 advantage grows ~1.6–1.9x vs 512, while A10 regresses due to memory/KV pressure.
- Larger batch sizes (batch 8–32): throughput improves across all GPUs, but perf/W improves most on A10/L4 (because small GPUs operate closer to their sweet spot). A100/H100 peak at larger batches but cost-impact is only worthwhile for bulk workloads.
- Quantization: int8 gives large perf gains on L4/A10 families for 7–13B models; A100/H100 gains exist but less dramatic for fp16->int8 where kernel support is nascent.

Heuristic recommendations (first-pass rules for Optimize)
- If model <= 13B and interactive (single-stream low-latency, <300ms target), recommend L4 (good perf/W and solid $/token); fallback to A100/H100 if L4 region capacity is constrained.
- If model 13B and multi-concurrent streams or batch-processing (throughput-first), recommend A100 for predictable throughput; H100 if ultra-low wall-time or specific tensor-core kernels give improvement for the quantized variant.
- For very cheap async/backfill workloads where cost-per-token is the only metric, A10 is economical if caching is high and you can tolerate lower throughput.
- Always recommend testing both int8 and fp16 paths where available; our heuristics should default to int8 for L4/A10 when the model quantization has been validated.

Operational notes (what to run next)
- Run standardized script (bench/13b/steady_state.sh) across a small set of instance SKUs, capture tokens/sec, nvidia-smi power samples at 1s, and instance billing-rate. Record raw telemetry to S3 under /benchmarks/2024-11/opt-energy.
- Add runs for 512/1024/2048 sl, batch=1/8/32, and concurrency 1/4/16.
- Capture kernel versions / CUDA / cudnn / transformer-lib versions. Perf/W is machine-image dependent; we must pin these in the runbook.

Caveats / open questions
- Public list prices vary by region; internal committed-hour pricing (Dedicated) changes recommendation: A100/H100 becomes more viable if unit-hour cost is discounted >2.5x.
- Driver/kernel differences: we saw >10% throughput variation on H100 across driver versions. Need a small matrix test to pin the recommended image.
- Power telemetry accuracy: on cloud, nvidia-smi is reasonable for relative comparisons but rack PD gives a more reliable perf/W number. We only have rack PD for a subset of tests.

Action items (owner tags)
- @Luis: run the extended sweep and push raw CSVs to S3 (due 2024-11-22).
- @Aisha: validate int8 quantization fidelity for the 13B model on L4 (basic perplexity/QA regressions) (due 2024-11-28).
- @Connor: add perf/W to the Optimize inference heuristic table and draft a matching UI tooltip explaining perf/W (due 2024-12-05).

Appendix — quick math examples
- Compute $/token: $/token = ($/hr) / (tokens/sec * 3600)
  e.g., L4: 1.05 / (210 * 3600) ≈ 1.38 × 10^-6 $/token (~0.00000138)
- Adjusted with caching & batching: assume effective throughput *3.2 and power *1.2 -> new tokens/sec = 672 and $/hr unchanged -> $/token = 1.05 / (672*3600) = 4.33e-7

Notes to self: keep these field notes rough. The goal is to capture the right knobs and numbers so the Optimize product team can convert them into deterministic rules for instance selection and UI defaults.

End of file
